Dear valued stakeholders,
On behalf of the Board of Directors and the Management Team, I am privileged to present Annual Report for the ﬁnancial year 2025-26. This year has been a deﬁning chapter in Bank’s journey, a period where we did not just navigate the evolving economic landscape, but actively reshaped the strategies to emerge stronger, more agile, and more purposeful than ever before.
The Macroeconomic Landscape
 
The global economy in FY 2025–26 has operated under a cloud of shifting trade policies and geopolitical complexities. While the world saw a moderate expansion with Global GDP growth estimated at approximately 3.1 per cent, the momentum remained uneven across regions. The Emerging Market Economies (EMEs) faced headwinds of US Tariff and ﬂuctuating energy costs due to West Asia Crisis, yet the global narrative was one of cautious adaptability.
  

  
On Domestic Front, India has ﬁrmly established itself as the global engine of growth. Despite the external volatility as well as uncertainties, our domestic economy remained a "bright spot," with GDP clocking the impressive growth of ~7.6%1. This performance was fuelled by robust domestic consumption and sustained public-sector investment in infrastructure over the year. This favourable domestic tailwind provided the stable foundation for the growth.
The strong GDP growth, underpinned by inclusive economic drivers, demonstrates the nation’s ongoing transformation towards a more prosperous and self-reliant future. The focus on infrastructure and domestic demand not only strengthens the economy today but also sets the stage for India to realise its aspiration of becoming a leading global powerhouse by 2047, as envisaged under the “Viksit Bharat” mission. As the nation moves toward a $5 trillion economy by FY 2027-28, the Bank remains at the forefront of this journey.
Innovation is our tool, but customer service is our purpose.

Credit growth was broad-based, led by services, personal loans, agriculture and industry. The agriculture sector grew by 15.7 per cent, industry by 15.0 per cent (mainly MSMEs), services by 19.0 per cent and personal loans by 16.2 per cent. The Banking sector posted the record proﬁtability with PSBs showing an all-time high Net Proﬁt of `1.98 Lakh Crore in FY 2025–26.

The Bank’s Global Business demonstrated satisfactory growth as it grew to `29.70 Lakh Crore with Global Advances at `12.59 Lakh Crore and Global Deposit at `17.11 Lakh Crore. Current Deposits of the Bank was at `79,294 Crore while Savings Deposits was at `5.30 Lakh Crore. CASA Deposits as on 31st March, 2026 stood at `6.10 Lakh Crore as against `5.74 Lakh Crore as on 31st March, 2025. The Domestic CASA Share was at 37.0 per cent as on 31st March, 2026. During FY 2025-26, the Bank focused on giving impetus to granular growth and focused on retail customers for liability products by revamping Saving account products with attractive and innovative features for all the segments of customers viz., Salary, Defence personnel, Minors, Youth, Farmers, Women, Pensioners and Senior Citizens to provide a more personalized and modern banking experience to the customers.
Agriculture Advances demonstrated growth of 10.7 per cent to `2.00 Lakh Crore as on 31st March, 2026, compared to `1.81 Lakh Crore as on 31st March, 2025. The Bank’s continued focus on agricultural lending reﬂects its commitment to supporting rural economic development and inclusive growth.

Agriculture Advances demonstrated growth of 10.7 per cent to `2.00 Lakh Crore as on 31st March, 2026, compared to `1.81 Lakh Crore as on 31st March, 2025. The Bank’s continued focus on agricultural lending reﬂects its commitment to supporting rural economic development and inclusive growth.
On the Cyber Security front, the Bank had organised Hackathon 2025 with IIT Kanpur, themed “Code Against Malware” underscoring the dedication towards innovation and prevention. It was aimed at proactively devising solutions to address emerging cyber threats.
Asset quality improved signiﬁcantly as PSBs registered lowest ever NPAs, with the Gross NPA ratio declining to 1.93 per cent and the Net NPA ratio dropping to 0.39 per cent as on 31st March, 2026.
MSME Advances witnessed robust expansion, growing by 19.9 per cent to `1.95 Lakh Crore as on 31st March, 2026, from `1.63 Lakh Crore as on 31st March, 2025.
The Bank became the ﬁrst Public Sector Bank (PSB) to transition its corporate website to the "bank.in" domain, thereby enhancing cybersecurity, preventing fraud, and fostering greater trust among stakeholders.

Structural & Strategic Realignment

Structural & Strategic Realignment
To better serve our diverse clientele and improve operational efﬁciency, we have undertaken a comprehensive reorganization of our business verticals and credit delivery mechanisms. In alignment with the National 'Startup India' initiative, we launched a dedicated scheme for startups and inaugurated our ﬁrst specialized Startup Branch at Bhikaji Cama Place, New Delhi. This branch acts as a hub for tailored banking solutions, providing entrepreneurs with the ﬁnancial velocity they need to scale.
Managing Risks Concerns
Banks face heightened risks from rapid digitisation, including cyber threats, operational disruptions, and advanced fraud. Key challenges include staying compliant with evolving regulations, reducing NPAs, and securing digital payments.
Furthermore, the Bank remained vigilant regarding cyber concerns and implemented robust measures to monitor the risk of cyber and digital frauds. In FY 2025-26, concerted efforts were also undertaken to reinforce cyber security through targeted initiatives.

Advancing Digital Transformation Through Innovative Solutions
In FY 2025-26, the Bank reafﬁrmed its dedication to digitalisation. The Bank signiﬁcantly upgraded its Mobile Banking and Internet Banking platforms, now offering over 350 features. These enhancements have been thoughtfully designed to cater to diverse customer needs and preferences, ensuring banking services are more accessible, ﬂexible, and user-friendly.
The Bank places strong emphasis on risk management, backed by a robust IT and Information Security Risk Management Framework to identify, assess, and mitigate IT risks. Additionally, dedicated Artiﬁcial Intelligence (AI) & Machine Learning (ML) Governance and Risk Management frameworks address emerging risks in these domains.

Shri M. Paramasivam joined the Bank as an Executive Director on 1st December 2022. He is presently the domain Executive Director overseeing Corporate Credit, RAM (Retail, Agriculture, MSME and Mid-Corporate) Credit, Treasury & International Banking, and Financial Inclusion.

His expertise encompasses the entire gamut of banking, including Credit, Priority Sector, Forex & Trade Finance, Compliance, and Branch Banking.

Global Economy
The global economy has been marked by rising uncertainty in the past 5-6 years due to successive shocks. In 2025, the global economy faced trade tariffs, fragmentation and geopolitical tensions, yet demonstrated resilience by registering annual growth of 3.4 per cent1, higher than the earlier projection of 3.2 per cent. While global manufacturing struggled due to weak external demand and high energy costs, the Services sector remained the global growth engine, fuelled by post- pandemic travel and the rapid scaling of Artificial Intelligence (AI) related professional services.

Indian Economy
Amid a global landscape marked by uncertainty and volatility, the Indian economy continues to remain a compelling story of resilience. While many major economies are facing recessionary concerns, India continues to be the fastest- growing major economy, supported by strong domestic fundamentals and strategic trade realignments.
Amid the ongoing conflict, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) projects the world economic growth to slow down to 3.1 per cent in 2026 and marginally recover to 3.2 per cent in 2027, but significantly slower than the 3.4 per cent yearly Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth in 2025.
India’s agricultural sector has displayed resilience, maintaining a steady growth trajectory largely propelled by the allied sector. Although traditional food grain production has seen consistent gains in recent years, higher-value segments, including livestock, fisheries, and horticulture are now playing a transformative role. These allied industries have become central to enhancing rural income opportunities and ensuring long-term economic stability for farm households.
Economic fortunes across the globe are becoming increasingly divergent because of these pressures. Emerging markets and developing nations are bearing the brunt of the heightened volatility, with growth projections for these regions downgraded to 3.9 per cent in 2026 from 4.4 per cent in 2025.

India enters FY 2026–27 with strong momentum, having recorded an impressive growth rate of 7.6 per cent in the previous year (FY 2025–26)2. For the current FY 2026-27, major institutions have slightly moderated their forecasts to account for global volatility. The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) projects GDP growth at 6.9 per cent, while the IMF and World Bank have pegged it at 6.5 per cent and 6.6 per cent respectively.
The global economic recovery experienced another setback in February’2026 as US and Israel attacked Iran and conflict spread across West Asia. The event has introduced profound uncertainty and disrupted global trade routes and energy supplies due to blockade of Strait of Hormuz. This has led to significant rise in energy prices and freight cost that is severely impacting economies around the globe.

In contrast, advanced economies like the United States have shown relative resilience, maintaining a growth forecast of 2.3 per cent in 2026, higher than 2.1 per cent in 2025. Though even there, the return to inflation targets is expected to be slower. The Eurozone remains in a precarious position, hampered by high energy costs and modest growth forecast of only 1.1 per cent in 2026, lower than 1.4 per cent GDP growth in 2025. Amidst this uneven landscape, India continues to stand out as a notable exception, maintaining fastest growth rate compared to its regional peers.
The services sector, especially IT, Business Services, and Global Capability Centres (GCCs) remains a major growth engine. Services exports have been expanding strongly, supported by digitalization, AI driven solutions and global outsourcing trends.

In FY 2025-26, the Indian banking sector grappled with a record-high Credit- Deposit (CD) ratio, which surged to an all- time peak of 83 per cent by March 20264. This escalation is driven by a persistent divergence where robust credit growth, hovering between 13.5 and 14.5 per cent has consistently outpaced sluggish deposit accretion of roughly 10 – 11 per cent. As households increasingly pivot their savings toward higher-yielding equity markets and mutual funds, banks are facing a structural liquidity squeeze, forcing them to bridge the funding gap through expensive certificates of deposit and short-term market borrowings. This "funding stress" has become RBI’s primary regulatory concern, as an elevated CD ratio not only thins out Banks’ Net Interest Margins but also puts constraint on capacity of lenders to lend and support India's broader economic expansion.

In a significant shift, the RBI cumulatively reduced the repo rate by 125 basis points since February 2025, bringing it to 5.25 per cent. While this has spurred borrowing, it has put pressure on Net Interest Margins (NIMs) of Banks as loans linked to the repo rate are repriced immediately, the deposits get repriced with a lag as and when they mature.

A strong risk and compliance culture is fundamental to our operations and ensures the safety and soundness of our business. To continually assess and enhance this culture, the Bank conducts periodical employee surveys to evaluate awareness and engagement with risk and compliance practices. The results of these surveys are analyzed, and action plans are developed to address any gaps and strengthen our approach. Our comprehensive training programs and an incentive/disincentive framework aligned with our risk appetite, help ensure adherence to our risk management principles.

To effectively manage IT risk, the Bank deploys a comprehensive lifecycle of identification, measurement, monitoring, and mitigation. Key operational activities include regular risk assessments of critical applications and the active monitoring of systemic Risk Indicators (RIs) and Key Risk Indicators (KRIs).

The Bank also has put in place comprehensive Policy on Stress Testing to identify the vulnerabilities and assess capital/liquidity requirements under adverse but plausible scenarios. Stress tests are conducted across whole gamut of risks namely Credit risk, Market risk, Operational risk, Concentration risk, Interest Rate Risk in the Banking Book (IRRBB), Liquidity risk, Country risk, Group risk, Pension Obligation risk, etc. on a regular basis. Impacts estimated in stress testing exercise serves as an input in capital planning exercise of the Bank. Funding requirements under liquidity stress scenarios are also used for setting objectives of Contingency funding plans.

Statement by director responsible for the business responsibility report, highlighting ESG related challenges, targets and achievements (listed entity has flexibility regarding the placement of this disclosure). At Punjab National Bank, ESG has grown from a regulatory mandate to a key pillar of its corporate strategy. Our commitment to ESG integration continues to guide strategic evolution. Moving beyond conventional risk management, we are embedding sustainability metrics into our core lending and investment frameworks. By aligning our strategies with decarbonisation objectives and inclusive growth, we are transitioning towards a value-driven and sustainable banking framework. Our focus on transparency and ethical governance ensures that investment and lending practices contribute to a resilient, inclusive and equitable future. Through the Business Responsibility and Sustainability Reporting (BRSR) framework, we strengthen accountability and uphold high standards of governance and environmental sustainability. Responsible banking, for us, is not optional, it is the foundation that guides business decisions and supports our contribution to a low-carbon, sustainable future. During the year, the Bank strengthened its environmental initiatives under "Palaash 3.0", with a focused approach towards green financing, sustainable resource management and reduction in carbon footprint. Our commitment to environmentally responsible banking is reflected through initiatives such as biodegradable credit card, green products including Green Home Loans. The Bank has also set a long-term goal of achieving net zero emissions by 2060, in alignment with national climate commitments. On the social front, the Bank remains committed to inclusive growth and community engagement.

Initiatives “PNB Sampark” continues to enhance outreach and accessibility, while the introduction of the Braille Credit Card reflects our focus on inclusivity (for visually impaired customers). The ‘Unnati Path’ program, along with the engagement of Indian women’s cricket captain Ms. Harmanpreet Kaur as Bank’s first female brand ambassador symbolizes our commitment to women empowerment and progressive values. The Bank also promotes employee engagement through initiatives such as PNB Khel Utsav and Taal Tarang. Employees well-being is further supported through initiatives like ‘PNB Sparsh’, providing access to professional psychological support. We continue to support self-employment and rural development through Farmer Training Centres, FLCs, RSETIs and Rural Development centers, along with financial literacy initiatives for farmers, SHGs and MSMEs. Our continued financing to Self-Help Groups embolden grassroots entrepreneurship and contributes to social upliftment. From a governance perspective, the Bank continues to uphold the highest standards of transparency, ethical conduct and accountability. Robust internal controls, strong compliance frameworks and continuous capacity building through structured training programmes reinforce governance practices across all levels. Specialized training on climate risk, renewable energy and green financing are equipping employees to align with evolving sustainability priorities, while initiatives such as the “Cyber Run” create awareness and strengthen organizational engagement. The Bank’s efforts culminated to several prestigious awards and recognitions, including the Best BFSI Brands-ET Edge, CIMS ME Banking Excellence Awards for Best Bank in implementing Government Schemes and the Best MSME Friendly Bank category.

The Bank was honored with the 21st IBA Banking Technology Awards for Fintech, DPI Adoption and Digital Financial Inclusion. Additionally, the Golden Peacock National Training Award and the Institutional Excellence Award, reflect excellence in workforce development and knowledge integration.

Yes. The Bank has an equal opportunity policy as per the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016. Equal opportunity means that all employees experience fairness, impartiality and equal access to all career initiatives at workplace. It promotes an inclusive work environment that values and accepts the diverse, cultural and social background of its staffs. Punjab National Bank is committed to create an inclusive workplace which provides equal opportunities in employment and where every employee is treated with respect and dignity. The Equal Opportunity Policy is applicable to all Branches/Offices of Punjab National Bank located in India and covers all persons with disability and acquiring disability during service period / work tenure in the Bank. Inherent Limitations of Internal Financial Controls over Financial Reporting
Opinion

Opinion
Because of the inherent limitations of internal financial controls over financial reporting, including the possibility of collusion or improper management override of controls, material misstatements due to error or fraud may occur and not be detected. Also, projections of any evaluation of the internal financial controls over financial reporting to future periods are subject to the risk that the internal financial controls over financial reporting may become inadequate because of changes in conditions, or that the degree of compliance with the policies or procedures may deteriorate.
We have audited the internal financial controls over financial reporting of Punjab National Bank (“the Bank”) as of 31 March, 2026 in conjunction with our audit of the Standalone Financial Statements of the Bank for the year ended on that date which includes internal financial controls over financial reporting of the Bank’s branches/offices.
We believe that the audit evidence we have obtained and the audit evidence obtained by the branch auditors, in terms of their reports referred to in the Other Matters paragraph below, is sufficient and appropriate to provide a basis for our unqualified audit opinion on the Bank’s internal financial controls over financial reporting.

2.c Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR)
In the Indian context, the guidelines for NSFR were effective from October 1, 2021. The NSFR is defined as the amount of available stable funding relative to the amount of required stable funding. “Available stable funding” (ASF) is defined as the portion of capital and liabilities expected to be reliable over the time horizon considered by the NSFR, which extends to one year. The amount of stable funding required ("Required stable funding") (RSF) of a specific institution is a function of the liquidity characteristics and residual maturities of the various assets held by that institution as well as those of its off-balance sheet (OBS) exposures. The Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR) and Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) are significant components of the Basel III reforms. The LCR guidelines which promote short term resilience of a bank’s liquidity profile have been issued vide circular DOR. LRG.No.82/13-10-001/2025-26, dated November 28, 2025. The NSFR guidelines on the other hand ensure reduction in funding risk over a longer time horizon by requiring banks to fund their activities with sufficiently stable sources of funding in order to mitigate the risk of future funding stress.

Now I request MD sir for his opening remarks.
Ashok Chandra: Good evening, ladies and gentlemen. First of all, I would like to touch upon the state of Indian
economy. Indian economy continues to demonstrate a strong underlying growth momentum,
supported by resilient domestic demand, infrastructure investment, expanding services activity,
and a steadily strengthening financial system.
India recorded real GDP growth of 7.8% in the first quarter of FY26-27 compared with 6.9% in
the corresponding quarter of the previous year. Recently, MPC in its meeting and World Bank
in its India Development report had also revised the GDP estimates for financial year FY26-27
to 7.1% from the previous estimates of 6.7% and 6.6%, respectively.
On the external front, India's Merchandise exports grew by 17.85% Y-o-Y during the period
April to August 2026, reaching an estimated US$215.91 billion. The banking sector
characterized by historically low levels of stressed assets and strong profitability is well
positioned to play a pivotal role in supporting and sustaining India's economic expansion.
Coming to Punjab National Bank, we sustained a strong business momentum in Q2, marked by
a decisive improvement in margins in line with our expectations, continued strengthening of

asset quality and enhanced operating efficiency. Our performance reflects the strength of our
franchise and disciplined execution of strategic priorities. We remain firmly on track to deliver
our FY26-27 guidance.
Our focus on retail, agriculture, and MSME continues to guide our efforts towards building a
diversified and resilient advances book. At the beginning of the financial year, we have targeted
to open 250 branches in this financial year with particular emphasis on strengthening our
footprint in the Southern and Western regions.
We have already opened 162 branches out of which 119 are in the Southern and Western region.
In parallel, we are accelerating our digital transformation to build a more agile, efficient, and
customer-centric organization. Our investments in technology, process automation and data
analytics are aimed at simplifying banking journeys, improving service delivery, and enhancing
productivity while positioning the bank to scale efficiency in a rapidly evolving banking
environment.
With this context, let me now turn to the segment-wise performance and key developments
during the quarter. First, I will touch on the overall business growth. Our gross global business
has reached INR 31.18 lakh crores, registering a robust Y-o-Y growth of 11.9%.

has reached INR 31.18 lakh crores, registering a robust Y-o-Y growth of 11.9%.
Our advances grew by 14.7% Y-o-Y to INR 13.41 lakh crores despite reducing IBPC exposure
by INR 23,700 crores. Excluding this impact, core advances registered a robust Y-o-Y growth
of 17.4%, reflecting healthy credit demand and strong underlying business momentum. Our core
RAM portfolio continued to deliver healthy growth with retail advances, excluding IBPC
growing by 16.3%, MSME by 19.8%, and agriculture (priority sector) by 18.1% Y-o-Y,
reflecting broad-based traction across key segments.
Credit growth is well positioned to maintain its strong momentum, supported by a robust
sanction pipeline. Bank sanctioned INR 4 lakh crores in FY 2025-26 in corporate credit lines.
Further, in the first half of this year, we have already crossed more than INR 2.5 lakh crores of
sanctions in the corporate credit. Our pipeline credit is to the tune of INR 1.58 lakh crores,
which provides a strong visibility for future credit growth.
Global deposits of the bank have reached to INR 17.77 lakh crores with Y-o-Y growth of 9.9%.
Our CASA strategy is centered on deepening customer engagements and enhancing individual
saving account balance, which grew by 8.1% Y-o-Y. In the beginning of FCNR campaign, we
had targeted to raise USD 2.5 billion, and we have raised USD2.7 billion in a calibrated manner.

Accordingly, our deposit mobilization remains measured and strategic with a clear emphasis on

I will touch upon the profitability. Improving profitability remains the bank's foremost strategic
priority as consistently emphasized across various forums. As indicated in our previous
interaction, we had expected a sequential improvement in margins during FY 2026-27. Our Q2

Domestic NIM improved by 10 basis points sequentially from 2.64% to 2.74%, while global
NIM increased from 2.5% to 2.58%. We expect this positive trajectory to strengthen further in
the coming quarters, supported by disciplined balance sheet optimization. NII increased to INR
11,601 crores, registering Y-o-Y growth of 10.8% and sequential growth of 7.4%, surpassing
our stated guidance of 7%.
Operating profit is continuously above INR 7,500 crores mark from the last 3 quarters and
stands at INR 7,532 crores for Q2 of this year. Core operating profit, excluding recoveries from
written-off accounts and treasury gains, grew by 29.4% Y-o-Y basis and 8% on a Q-o-Q basis.
Core operating profit forms 79% of the total operating profit in Q2 of FY2027, which was 64%
in Q2 of FY26.
Our fee-based income grew by 16% on Y-o-Y basis, reflecting continued progress in
diversifying revenue sources. The bank recorded a net profit of INR 5,532 crores in Q2 with Y-
o-Y growth of 12.8%. The bank's overall earnings profile reflects a sustained focus on profitable
growth and strengthening core earnings.
Efficiency ratios. Our return on assets has consistently remained above 1% mark and stands at

Efficiency ratios. Our return on assets has consistently remained above 1% mark and stands at
1.05% in Q2 of this year. Our return on equity stands at 17.32%. Our tangible book value per
share stood at INR 111.94 as on September 30, 2026, registering a significant improvement over
INR 95.92 as on September 30, 2025.
Our cost-to-income ratio has demonstrated a consistent declining trend, improving to 50.45% in
Q2 from 51.20% in Q2 of last year, reflecting our continued focus on operational efficiency and
cost optimization. I will touch upon the asset quality.
Asset quality continues to strengthen with the gross NPA ratio declined to 2.55% as on
September 30, 2026 from 3.45% as on 30th September 2026. The net NPA ratio has also
improved to 0.25% as of September 30, 2026 from 0.36% as on 30th September 2025. This
sustained improvement reflects our disciplined credit underwriting, robust monitoring, and
focused recovery efforts while keeping us firmly on track to achieve our FY26-27 guidance on
both GNPA and net NPA.
We have not seen any material impact of geopolitical tensions on the bank's asset quality. Our
slippages remain contained, SMA accounts are stable, and the overall credit portfolio continues
to perform well. Our SMA-0, 1, and 2 all combined, is all-time low levels of 2.50% of the overall

past few quarters. Do you expect to purchase any PSL certificates in the next year?

under that PSLC. And I'm expecting that at least around 50 to 60 basis point cut should be
happening in the next year. More than that, we are already targeting in that direction now. And
we are already compliant as far the RBI regulatory guidelines are concerned. We don't have any
issues related with the PSLC compliant. Your -- another question was related with?

have changed. One is the repo rate cut, which I assume would have had an impact of about 5, 6,

this quarter, but I assume that would have a negligible impact because TD rates take time to pass
through. So what exactly changed as per your earlier expectation?
